you should aim to complete the content by the indicated dates.

**Experiment programming**

The following repository contains code designed to introduce
the basics of programming behavioural experiments in Python.

`https://github.com/crossley/crossleylab/tree/main/code/behavioural_experiment_progression`

This sequence progresses from drawing stimuli and handling
timing and input to implementing state-based control of
behaviour. The scripts demonstrate how input, timing, and
display updates combine to form structured experimental
tasks, culminating in complete behavioural experiments such
as action selection, category learning, and reaching tasks.
Advanced examples demonstrate efficient visual stimulus
generation using NumPy.


## Introduction to dynamical systems

Please aim to complete by the end of Week 5.

`https://github.com/crossley/crossleylab/tree/main/code/electrochemical_signals_progression`

These scripts progress from numerical integration (Euler’s
method) to particle-based simulations of diffusion across a
membrane, adding selective channels and electrical forces to
illustrate electrochemical gradients. Later examples convert
ion imbalance across a membrane into a simple
resting-potential–like signal, providing a visual and
computational introduction to membrane potentials and
electrochemical signalling.


## Models of single neurons

Please aim to complete by the end of Week 7.

Tutorial 6 develops a detailed understanding of the
Hodgkin–Huxley neuron by implementing the full model,
examining the behaviour of activation and inactivation
gates, and exploring how membrane dynamics change as
biophysical parameters are varied. Students reproduce key
figures to build intuition for how conductances and reversal
potentials shape action potentials, and then investigate how
different current injections produce single spikes or spike
trains. The focus is on understanding how cellular
mechanisms give rise to excitability through simulation and
parameter exploration.

Tutorial 7 moves from biophysically detailed models to
simpler dynamical neuron models, focusing on the Izhikevich
and quadratic integrate-and-fire formulations. Students
reproduce canonical firing patterns, analyse oscillatory
behaviour mathematically, and examine conditions under which
simplified models are equivalent to integrate-and-fire
neurons. The emphasis is on connecting dynamical systems
analysis with reduced neuron models used in large-scale
simulations.

- <a href="tutorials/tutorial_6.html" target="_blank">Tutorial 6</a>
- <a href="tutorials/tutorial_7.html" target="_blank">Tutorial 7</a>


## Building networks

Please aim to complete by the end of Week 8.

`https://github.com/crossley/crossleylab/tree/main/code/basal_ganglia_spiking_network`

This repository introduces network-level modelling using a
spiking basal ganglia circuit. The code demonstrates how
single-neuron dynamics extend to interacting populations,
including excitatory and inhibitory connections, structured
connectivity, and population-level dynamics emerging from
local interactions. The emphasis is on understanding how
action selection and competition can arise from network
structure rather than single-neuron behaviour alone.


## Synaptic plasticity

Please aim to complete by the end of Week 9.

This section introduces learning rules that modify synaptic
strength over time. Hebbian learning is used to illustrate
how correlations between activity can shape connectivity,
while reinforcement learning introduces reward-dependent
plasticity and credit assignment. The goal is to connect
plasticity mechanisms with changes in network behaviour and
learning over repeated experience.


## Models for your final project

Please aim to complete by the end of Week 13.

`https://github.com/crossley/crossleylab/tree/main/code/basal_ganglia_spiking_network_cat_learn`

This repository combines the earlier components of the
course into a full computational model that links neural
dynamics, network interactions, and learning. The model
demonstrates how basal ganglia circuitry and reinforcement
learning mechanisms can support procedural category
learning, providing a reference framework for final
projects.
